seoDescription: Learn how to set up the foundation for a robust Access Control List (ACL) in Laravel by configuring the database for user roles. This tutorial covers creating the necessary tables for users, roles, and a pivot table to manage the many-to-many relationship. You'll see how to use Artisan commands to generate models, migrations, and seeders. Discover how to define Eloquent relationships, seed your database with default roles (User, Author, Admin), and programmatically assign these roles to users.

chapters.title: Database Schema for Roles
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the three-table database schema required for a many-to-many user role relationship and uses Artisan to create the Role model and migration.

chapters.title: Defining the Role Migration and Model Relationships
chapters.description: This chapter covers adding fields to the roles migration and defining the 'belongsToMany' relationship in both the User and Role Eloquent models.

chapters.title: Creating the Pivot Table Migration
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to create the 'user_role' pivot table migration, define its columns, and explains Laravel's default naming conventions.

chapters.title: Customizing the Eloquent Relationship
chapters.description: This chapter shows how to explicitly define the pivot table name and foreign keys in the 'belongsToMany' relationship method to override Laravel's defaults.

chapters.title: Seeding Default Roles
chapters.description: This chapter walks through creating a seeder to populate the database with default 'User', 'Author', and 'Admin' roles.

chapters.title: Assigning Roles to Users in a Seeder
chapters.description: This chapter explains how to modify the user seeder to attach the previously created roles to each user using the 'attach' method.

chapters.title: Finalizing Seeding and Running Migrations
chapters.description: This chapter finalizes the user seeder by assigning the correct roles to the author and admin, then executes the migrations and seeders together.

chapters.title: Verifying the Database Setup
chapters.description: This final chapter uses a database client to inspect the 'users', 'roles', and 'user_role' tables to confirm the data was migrated and seeded correctly.

summary:
## Database Architecture for ACL

To implement user roles, a **many-to-many relationship** is required. This involves three database tables:

*   `users`: Stores user information (already exists in Laravel).
*   `roles`: Stores the available roles (e.g., Admin, Author, User).
*   `user_role`: A **pivot table** that links users to roles, containing a `user_id` and a `role_id` for each assignment.

## Laravel Migrations & Models

1.  **Create Role Model & Migration**: Use the Artisan command `php artisan make:model Role -m` to generate both the `Role` model and its corresponding migration file.
2.  **Define Roles Table**: In the `roles` migration, add string columns for `name` and `description`.
3.  **Create Pivot Table Migration**: Use `php artisan make:migration create_user_role_table` to create the migration for the pivot table. This table should contain integer columns for `user_id` and `role_id`.

> [!NOTE]
> Laravel uses conventions for naming. A pivot table connecting `user` and `role` models is expected to be named `user_role` (singular, alphabetical order). The foreign key columns are expected to be `user_id` and `role_id`.

## Eloquent Many-to-Many Relationships

To define the relationship in your models, use the `belongsToMany` method.

*   **In `User.php`**:
    ```php
    public function roles() {
        return $this->belongsToMany(App\Role::class);
    }
    ```
*   **In `Role.php`**:
    ```php
    public function users() {
        return $this->belongsToMany(App\User::class);
    }
    ```

> [!TIP]
> You can override Laravel's naming conventions by passing additional arguments to the `belongsToMany` method. The second argument is the pivot table name, the third is the foreign key of the current model, and the fourth is the foreign key of the related model.
> 
> `return $this->belongsToMany(App\Role::class, 'user_role', 'user_id', 'role_id');`

## Seeding Data

1.  **Create a Seeder**: Use `php artisan make:seeder RoleTableSeeder` to create a file for seeding default roles.
2.  **Populate Roles**: Inside the `run()` method of `RoleTableSeeder`, create and save new instances of the `Role` model for 'User', 'Author', and 'Admin'.
3.  **Update DatabaseSeeder**: In `DatabaseSeeder.php`, call your new seeder. The order is critical.
    ```php
    $this->call(RoleTableSeeder::class);
    $this->call(UserTableSeeder::class); // Must run after roles are created
    ```

## Assigning Roles to Users

In the `UserTableSeeder`, after a user is created and saved, you can assign a role using the `attach()` method on the relationship.

1.  **Retrieve Roles**: Fetch the role models you need from the database (e.g., `Role::where('name', 'user')->first();`).
2.  **Attach Role**: Access the relationship method (with parentheses) and call `attach()`.
    ```php
    $user->roles()->attach($role_user);
    ```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A user model **must be saved** to the database before you can attach a role. The `attach()` method needs the `user_id` to create the entry in the pivot table, and the ID is only generated upon saving.

## Final Execution

Run `php artisan migrate --seed` to create all tables and populate them with the data defined in your migrations and seeders. You can then verify the `users`, `roles`, and `user_role` tables in a database client to confirm the relationships are set up correctly.
transcription:
## Database Schema for Roles

I'm going to start implementing my roles by starting on the database and so by adding these roles, setting them up in the database. For this to work I will need three tables. I already got one, which is the user table which holds the users of course. I will have a table holding the roles, and then the third table will hold, well, kind of the matches where which basically it will hold a user ID and a role ID to match users with roles because this will be a many-to-many relationship. One user may have multiple roles, and one role can of course be assigned to multiple users. Therefore we need three tables.

I'm going to use the Artisan command to do this. So in my terminal video, I'm going to write `php artisan make:model` and first I want to create a Role model, `-m` to also create a migration file. As you can see, this added this Role.php file, this model file here, and it added this migration file.

## Defining the Role Migration and Model Relationships

Let's start with the migration. This is the well, boilerplate Laravel created for us. And I will need two additional fields here, both will be string fields: a name of the role and, well, though this isn't really used in this application to be honest, a description just to show how you could configure your roles. So this is all I need for the migration file here.

The next thing is I want to go to my Role.php model file here and I will set up the relation of this role to the user. And this will just be a public function which I will call `users()` because many, it's many users, and it will return `this->belongsToMany(App\User::class)`.

This is the relation because as I said my role may be assigned to many users, therefore it belongs to many users. On the other hand, in the User model here, I will, well, basically define the same but it is called `roles()` and this will be `return $this->belongsToMany(App\Role::class)`.

## Creating the Pivot Table Migration

Now we got this many-to-many relationship set up. The next step is to set up this matching table, this third table I was talking of. So again, back in the command line here I'm going to write `php artisan make:migration` and then I will call this `create_user_role_table`. As you see, this created this file here, this migration file, and inside this file I'll have to write a little bit more than in the other migration files. But I'm just going to copy this here from my Role migration file.

Down here I'll have `Schema::drop` and the table will be called `user_role` here. Of course, `user_role`. I will have increments, timestamps, that is fine. However here I will have an integer which will be called `user_id`, and I just copied this line because I'll have the same for, well, the `role_id`. The naming here is important because Laravel will look for a table called `user_role` and it will also look for `user` and `role_id` in this table when we actually use this relationship we set up in our model files here through Laravel's Eloquent model. So this is very important to understand.

## Customizing the Eloquent Relationship

Now you could change this default behavior by, when creating this relationship, adding additional parameters here where you could say... and let's actually do this even though it's not necessary here. We could say, okay, the matching table is called `user_role`. That's just the name I gave this table here, and as I said Laravel will infer this name by default, but if you have another table name that's no problem. Just specify it as an extra parameter.

And then as an additional parameter you can say, well the foreign key here in this case will be `user_id`. Also you might say, well the other key of my role will be `role_id`. Now I'm just going to copy all this and in my Role model file I'll insert this. And of course this has to be changed here in this order. So that's very important to understand, to get right. As I said, it wouldn't have been necessary here because that is the default Laravel infers, but whenever you change names this is the way to set it up.

## Seeding Default Roles

So with this out of the way, the next thing I want to do is I want to seed some data. I want to create some default roles which are always there when we start or create our application. So as I already got my `UserTableSeeder` which sets up my users, I will create a new seeder for, well, my roles. And I will again, oops, do this in the command line here by typing `php artisan make:seeder` and then I will just call this `RoleTableSeeder` and the name is purely up to you here.

So now this seeder here was added and as you can see it's just an empty `run` function. And inside this function, I will create the code which I want to run through upon seeding. Or, well yeah, when I basically run the seed command in the Artisan command line interface. What I actually want to see here is I will, well, say we have the role for a normal user which will be a new Role. And I will import it at the top, so we will use `App\Role`. So that I can just write `new Role` here. And while this role user, this user role, will have a name of, let's say, 'user', and it will have some kind of description, and I will just write 'A normal user'. And thereafter I will save this.

I'm going to quickly copy this and create two new users. The first one will be my author user here, `role_author`, and it will be called 'author' and here the description will be 'An author'. And then I will have my admin. That was the wrong key. I will have my admin here, `role_admin`, so that we get the three roles we need for our application to work.

Now the last thing is in the `DatabaseSeeder` file here, I will, well, basically uncomment it here because I already wrote it. But we have to call the `RoleTableSeeder` and then and thereafter the `UserTableSeeder`. Now the order here is important because I'm going to change the `UserTableSeeder` in a second.

## Assigning Roles to Users in a Seeder

Because in the `UserTableSeeder` where we set up our users, I also want to assign some basic roles to them. I'm currently not doing that, but I will do in a second. Therefore it's important to first create the roles so that we can then use them in the `UserTableSeeder`, which I'm doing now. Assigning roles is pretty easy.

First I'm going to retrieve my three roles by just saying, well, accessing the database through Eloquent, so with the Role model, and here just say well my user model is where the name equals 'user'. That's the name we just defined. And here I will get the first role, and I know I only have one so it just will fetch the only role I have, the user role. Now of course this will change to `role_author` here, and here it will be `role_admin`. And here I need to make these changes too. So this retrieves the roles.

And now to assign them to a user is super simple. Laravel allows me to do the following: I can access the user I'm creating here, or I already created and saved, and the order is important here again. It has to be saved to the database so that Laravel can actually create the relation. Because remember, we have this third table where we have the `role_id` and `user_id`. Laravel can only create an entry in this table which defines the actual relation if we have a role as well as a user in the database, because it needs the IDs of the user and the role. So we have to save the user and therefore write it to the database before assigning a role and hence creating the relation. That's very important and I hope it's clear why.

So what I'm doing here is I access the `roles` relation with parentheses here because we're still in the query. I'm not accessing it as a property where I then want to, let's say, loop through all the roles this user has, but instead I want to kind of create a chain statement if we were to translate this into SQL. So I use parentheses to say, now connect the user with the roles table here, and then I use the `attach` method Laravel provides me with the Eloquent model. And this allows me to attach a role because I'm accessing `roles` here to this user, and the role I want to attach is `role_user`. Now of course attach doesn't only work with roles and users, it would be the same behavior if you have posts and comments for example. This basically just says or tells Laravel to create a relation and to create this entry I was just talking about in this third table.

## Finalizing Seeding and Running Migrations

Now I just copy this here to my admin where I'm going to assign `role_admin`, and finally to my author here at the bottom where I assign `role_author`. Okay, so now let's write all the data to the database by running `php artisan migrate --seed` to also run the seeding after the tables have been created. Looks good.

## Verifying the Database Setup

And now what I did here, or what I do have here is I have my, well this is SQL Pro, which allows me to connect to my database and have a look at the contents. And as you can see I got my `roles`, `user_roles`, and `users` table. In the `users` table, I got my three users. In the `roles` table, I got the three roles I set up. And in the `user_role` table you can see I got the assignments of user 1 has role 1. And if we have a look, user 1 is the normal user, not the admin, not the author, and it has the role 1 which is the normal user role. So this works.

This is how we set up our database, how we seed the data. And in the next part we'll have a look at, well, the actual work: how we protect our middleware and how we restrict access based on these roles we just set up. See you there, bye.
